solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Notice one entering great church to dispense rites

indicators.note: something entering a building goes inside it, so the I goes inside the church

blocks.note: an ad is a notice in a paper
a minster is a large church, like York Minster

explanation.surface: A notice about a newcomer joining the cathedral clergy to conduct services.
explanation.walkthrough: 'great church' is one word, MINSTER, split open to take the I.
explanation.definitionFit: The set phrase of the priesthood: a priest administers the sacraments and the last rites.

clue.text: White dog ensnared by a plant

indicators.note: a creature ensnared by something is trapped inside it

blocks.note: the aster, a daisy-like garden flower

explanation.surface: A white dog tangled up in a flower bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The dog sits between 'a' and the plant, the order the clue gives them.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of a smooth pale stone, used as an adjective for pure white, as in alabaster skin.

clue.text: Changes M&S trousers for spouse returning socks

indicators.note: to trouser something is to pocket it, so M and S pocket everything else between them
something returning comes back the way it went, so PRO + MATE reads backwards

blocks.note: the two letters of the shop's name, M first and S last
PRO (for, as in pros and cons) + MATE (spouse)
hose is an old word for stockings or socks

explanation.surface: A shopper at Marks & Spencer buying trousers for a husband who is returning socks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trousers' is not clothing but a verb for pocketing, the way a thief trousers cash; M&S is the British store Marks & Spencer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the plural noun for transformations, as in Ovid's poem of shape-shifting gods.

clue.text: Vegetable energy upped swan absorbs

indicators.note: in a down clue, a word sent up is read from the bottom, so it is reversed
something that absorbs takes a thing into itself

blocks.note: a pen is a female swan

explanation.surface: A swan that gets a burst of energy from eating vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a Scottish word for a turnip or swede, eaten with haggis on Burns Night.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional use: the Scots name for a root vegetable, the turnip or swede.

clue.text: Workers in store go among bizarre Insta hosts

indicators.note: one thing placed among others sits in their midst
something bizarre is weird and out of its normal shape, so the letters of INSTA HOSTS take a new order

blocks.note: the ten letters rearranged, split around PASS
in a card game, to go is to pass your turn

explanation.surface: Staff being drafted in to front strange Instagram broadcasts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hosts' looks like a container signal but is part of the fodder; 'among' does the containing.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain description: the staff who serve customers in a shop, 'store' being its everyday synonym.

clue.text: Close to mate, black bishop in decline

indicators.note: the close of something is its end, so the close of 'mate' is its last letter

blocks.note: B = bishop, as in chess notation

explanation.surface: A chess game near checkmate, with the black bishop on the slide.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess picture of mate and a black bishop is only letters: the E ending 'mate', then two Bs.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from the tide: when the water goes out, it falls away and declines.

clue.text: Old Peruvian head touring a city almost put out of action

indicators.note: a tour goes round a place
almost the whole word means all but its last letter, so CITY loses its Y

blocks.note: the Inca empire ruled old Peru
pate is an old word for the head

explanation.surface: An ancient Inca chief going round a city that has nearly been knocked out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' reads as a leader of the Incas, but it is the body part, an old word for the top of the skull, opened after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to disable someone is to put them out of action.

clue.text: Part of speech: verb, adverb or adjective say

blocks.note: one of the word classes of grammar
'say' marks these as examples: think about what kind of word the name 'verb' is

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson listing the word classes.
explanation.walkthrough: The list seems to name parts of speech other than the answer, but the words 'verb', 'adverb' and 'adjective' are themselves nouns, the names of things.
explanation.definitionFit: Both halves hold: it is a word class, and every name of a word class belongs to it.

clue.text: Reactionary character in flagrante dancing tango?

indicators.note: dancers move around the floor, so the letters move into a new order

blocks.note: T is tango in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A scandalous tango, caught in the act, the Latin in flagrante.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tango' looks like the dance being done; it is only its letter T. Alf Garnett was the bigoted father in the 1960s-70s BBC sitcom Till Death Us Do Part.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by type: the TV bigot who ranted against change was a byword for reactionary views.

clue.text: Seaman to fall from grace with the drink

blocks.note: to sin is to fall from grace

explanation.surface: A sailor's moral downfall caused by drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the drink' reads as one noun phrase, but 'the' is a piece and 'drink' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a strong green aniseed spirit, once banned in France.

clue.text: Part of Britain lies at sea with fog swirling

indicators.note: someone at sea is confused, so the letters of LIES are muddled
something swirling spins round, so the letters of WITH FOG spin into a new order

explanation.surface: A stretch of Britain lying out at sea, wrapped in swirling fog.
explanation.walkthrough: Two separate anagrams side by side. 'with' looks like a link but is part of the second fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an island county off England's south coast.

clue.text: Check old song over for concert halls

indicators.note: a thing turned over is upside down

blocks.note: an air is a tune or song

explanation.surface: Reviewing an old song before booking concert venues.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the song is reversed; the O for old stays in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin plural: the halls where audiences sit, including for concerts.

clue.text: Peter Sellers holding tongue

indicators.note: the name holds letters inside it, and those letters are the answer

explanation.surface: The comic actor Peter Sellers biting his tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: The famous name is only a letter string; the answer runs across the gap between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A dated name for Gaelic, the language of the Scottish Highlands and Ireland; tongue means language.

clue.text: Fish around loch bite in sudden wintry spell

indicators.note: one thing around another encircles it

explanation.surface: A fish round a Scottish lake taking a bite during a frosty spell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish' reads as a verb for angling in the loch; it is the noun COD.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for a short burst of freezing weather that arrives without warning.

clue.text: Style artist recalled with Dail member and Green

indicators.note: something recalled is called back

blocks.note: a TD (Teachta Dala) sits in the Dail, the Irish parliament

explanation.surface: An artist remembered for working with an Irish politician from the Green party.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dail is the lower house of the Irish parliament and its members are TDs; 'Green' is the adjective ECO, not the party.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the geometric design movement of the 1920s and 30s.

clue.text: Old poem in book reversing virus misery?

indicators.note: a car reversing goes backwards, so FLU WOE is written backwards

blocks.note: flu is a virus, woe is misery

explanation.surface: An old poem in a book about the miseries of a virus, perhaps a plague tale.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark excuses the odd phrase 'virus misery', which is only two pieces to turn round.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Old English epic about a hero who kills the monster Grendel.

clue.text: Stable American coin no longer used

explanation.surface: A reliable American coin that has gone out of circulation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stable' looks like an adjective for the coin; it is the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a gold coin of the late Roman and Byzantine empire.

clue.text: Superb exterior to masculine perfection

indicators.note: what is exterior to something lies on its outside

explanation.surface: A superb exterior leading to manly perfection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exterior' is not a noun about looks but a positional instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the highest point anything can reach.

clue.text: Pale and sickly old rock-and-roller sought by police

blocks.note: a Teddy boy, a 1950s British youth who wore Edwardian dress and loved rock and roll

explanation.surface: A pale, sickly ageing rocker on the run from the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pale and sickly' is one piece, not two; the 'and' belongs to it.
explanation.definitionFit: The word printed on a police poster of a fugitive.

clue.text: Spy boss blocking route to send out signal

indicators.note: something blocking a road stands in the middle of it

blocks.note: M is the head of MI6 in the James Bond stories

explanation.surface: The head of the secret service standing in the way of an escape route to send out a message.
explanation.walkthrough: M, Bond's boss, is the standard crossword spymaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from radio and TV, where stations broadcast their signal.

clue.text: Mackintosh from Scots own company in desert

indicators.note: one thing in another is inside it

blocks.note: to rat is to desert, as rats leave a sinking ship

explanation.surface: A Scottish firm deserting its partners, with Mackintosh as the Scots surname.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mackintosh' looks like a Scottish name to go with 'Scots'; it is the coat. 'desert' is the verb RAT, not sand.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the mackintosh, named after its Scottish inventor, is a waterproof coat.

clue.text: Moist after toil, clothing finally discarded in debauched place

indicators.note: the final letter is thrown away, so WEAR loses its R
one thing in another is inside it

blocks.note: WEAR (clothing, as in menswear) minus its final R
a sty is a place of filth or debauchery

explanation.surface: Workers so hot after their labours that they strip off their clothes somewhere wild.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clothing' is the noun WEAR, as in sportswear, and 'finally discarded' strips its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: damp skin after hard physical work.

clue.text: Suspend player who’s paid villain

explanation.surface: Banning a professional footballer who is a crook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspend' reads as a sports ban on the player; it is the parliamentary sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A parliamentary term: to end a session of parliament without dissolving it.

clue.text: In addition to a balloon, a second

explanation.surface: Getting a second balloon on top of the first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'balloon' is the verb, to swell up, not the party object.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both phrases add one thing to another.

clue.text: Cause problems in new NHS strike: another war won about power?

annotation.answer: THROW A SPANNER IN THE WORKS

indicators.note: a new version of something is remade, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A headline about a new strike in the National Health Service, framed as yet another war over power.
explanation.walkthrough: The NHS is Britain's National Health Service; the whole news story is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a tool dropped into machinery jams it, so the phrase means sabotaging a plan.

clue.text: Warms up again and runs races to conserve energy

indicators.note: to conserve something is to keep it safe

explanation.surface: An athlete warming up again and pacing themselves through the heats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warms up' suggests a runner loosening up; it is food heated a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal definition: the prefix re- means again, as with leftovers put back in the oven.

clue.text: Individual copies returned by judge

indicators.note: something returned is sent back

explanation.surface: Individual copies sent back by a judge in a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copies' reads as a plural noun, but it is the verb APES.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: things kept apart, each on its own.

clue.text: Relative in brown sent back in time

indicators.note: something sent back returns the way it came

blocks.note: an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A relative in a brown suit going back in time.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'in' is a link; the second puts the reversed colour inside AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal term: kin through the male line, a relative on the father's side.

clue.text: Suggest union quite honest, restructured following report

indicators.note: something restructured is rebuilt in a new form, so the letters of QUITE HONEST take a new order
one thing following another comes after it

blocks.note: a report is a bang, a pop

explanation.surface: A trade union proposal made quite honestly after a critical report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'union' reads as a trade union; it is marriage. 'report' is the noise of a gun, not a document.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for proposing marriage, and marriage is a union.

clue.text: Alpine margay is out with small foxes?

indicators.note: a bone that is out is dislocated, so the letters are displaced into a new order

explanation.surface: A wild cat of the Alps prowling about with some little foxes.
explanation.walkthrough: A margay is a small South American wild cat, so the animal picture hides a flower. 'Alpine' is a noun: a mountain plant. 'is' belongs to the fodder, leaving 'out' to signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a cushion-forming rock plant grown in alpine gardens, and gardeners call such plants alpines.

clue.text: Infernal type came together with Greek characters in love

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: phi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A devilish figure meeting up with some Greeks in love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in love' looks like a romantic phrase; 'in' puts the letters in MET and 'love' is O.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the devil of the Faust legend, short for Mephistopheles.

clue.text: Again, light period of power couple losing millions

indicators.note: a thing losing something no longer has it, so ITEM goes without its M

explanation.surface: A power couple whose era is over, having lost their millions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'power couple' reads as one phrase; 'power' ends the first piece and 'couple' starts the second. M = millions.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal definition split in two: the prefix re- is 'again' and the verb is 'light'.

clue.text: Plover and otter eluded traps

indicators.note: something that traps a creature holds it inside, so the phrase holds the answer

explanation.surface: A plover and an otter both escaping the trappers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'traps' reads as a noun the animals avoided; it is the verb that holds the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a small wading bird of the plover family.

clue.text: Exceptional academic modelled Loch Ard shores

indicators.note: clay being modelled is pressed into a new shape, so the letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A brilliant scholar posing for a painting on the shores of Loch Ard.
explanation.walkthrough: Loch Ard is a lake in the Scottish Trossachs.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by type: the prestigious Oxford scholarship goes only to exceptional students.

clue.text: Burn, start to smoke, turn to dust

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: to moulder is to decay slowly to dust

explanation.surface: Something burning, beginning to smoke and crumbling to dust.
explanation.walkthrough: Every phrase stays in the fire picture, which is the disguise: only the S and MOULDER are pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: burning slowly with smoke but no flame.

clue.text: Office appointment: mark for later time

blocks.note: a post is an office or position

explanation.surface: An office meeting pushed back to a later time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Office appointment' reads as one meeting at work; the two words are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal definition: writing a future date on a cheque or document.

clue.text: Senior detectives excuse certain offence

explanation.surface: Senior police convinced of a crime by an excuse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'offence' looks like a crime in the police scene; it means taking offence, annoyance.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of taking offence: annoyance at being slighted.

clue.text: Literary faux pas Tom Sharpe suggests?

blocks.note: count the letters of the novelist's name and look for a word they could be rearranged from

explanation.surface: A literary gaffe hinted at by the comic novelist Tom Sharpe.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the name TOM SHARPE is an anagram of METAPHORS, so the name is what 'mixed metaphors' look like.
explanation.definitionFit: A stylistic blunder: combining images that clash, like nipping something in the bud before it snowballs.

clue.text: Red stone your Roman Catholic leader keeps

indicators.note: someone who keeps a thing holds it

blocks.note: yr is the abbreviation of your
the head of the Roman Catholic Church

explanation.surface: The Pope holding on to a red gem that belongs to you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' is not a first letter signal here; the Catholic leader is the whole word POPE.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a deep red garnet used as a gemstone.

clue.text: This to shorten line that woman records with Marvin?

blocks.note: Hank Marvin, guitarist of the Shadows

explanation.surface: A singer cutting a line to record with Hank Marvin.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'This to shorten line', a knot used to shorten a rope. Hank Marvin was lead guitarist of the British band the Shadows.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by use: a knot tied to take up slack in a rope, and sailors call rope line.

clue.text: Stress at home with sibling tense

explanation.surface: Stress at home from a tense brother or sister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stress' is the verb, to emphasise, and 'tense' is only the grammar abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to state something firmly and repeatedly.

clue.text: Place in Hilton Hotel involved in wine: litres imported

indicators.note: a thing involved in another is wrapped up in it

blocks.note: H is hotel in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A room at the Hilton hotel stocked with wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hilton' is not the hotel chain but James Hilton, whose novel Lost Horizon invented the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by source: the hidden Himalayan paradise in James Hilton's novel Lost Horizon.

clue.text: Much appreciated bandana collected by short seller

indicators.note: something collected by a person ends up held by them
a word cut short loses its end

blocks.note: a bandana is a large handkerchief, a hanky
a tout sells tickets on the street

explanation.surface: A street trader grateful for the bandana handed in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short seller' sounds like a stock market trader; it is a tout cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: An expression of gratitude, said when a favour is much appreciated.

clue.text: One from Glasgow hosts peer, good runner

explanation.surface: A Glaswegian entertaining a lord who is a fine athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'runner' means a racehorse, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A racing term: a horse in its second calendar year, and racehorses are called runners.

clue.text: Sincere art making money?

blocks.note: 'art' is the old verb, as in 'thou art': you are making money

explanation.surface: Honest art that makes a profit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'art' is not painting but the old verb: 'thou earnest' is 'thou art earning'. The question mark flags the archaic trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses hold: serious and heartfelt, and the old second-person form of the verb for making money.

clue.text: Main brew pulls in crew aboard carrier?

indicators.note: something that pulls in draws a thing inside it
a passenger aboard is on the vehicle

blocks.note: a brew is a cup of tea
to man a ship is to crew it
a donkey, a beast of burden

explanation.surface: A strong brew that attracts sailors aboard an aircraft carrier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' is the old poetic word for the sea, not 'chief'. 'carrier' is a donkey, not a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the stretch of ocean between Australia and New Zealand, and main is poetic for the open sea.

clue.text: Curse a boring song — Sabrina’s last

indicators.note: a drill boring into wood goes inside it
the last of a word is its final letter, so Sabrina gives A

explanation.surface: Cursing a dull song by Sabrina, her latest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' is not dull but drilling into.
explanation.definitionFit: A church term: a formal curse of excommunication.

clue.text: Last presentation with old puns dreadful in effect

indicators.note: something dreadful is a mess, so the letters are messed into a new order

explanation.definitionFit: An idiom meaning virtually, for every practical purpose.

clue.text: Perhaps Amazon Go at first is stocking stakes

a shop stocking goods holds them

clue.text: Disheartened songwriter and musician

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle

explanation.surface: A dispirited songwriter who is also a musician.

explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a player of the lyre, the harp of ancient Greece.

clue.text: Egyptian god restraining explosive goddess

explanation.surface: An Egyptian god holding back a volatile goddess.
explanation.walkthrough: The first deity is only wordplay; the goddess at the end is the answer, from Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Titan mother of Zeus in Greek myth.

clue.text: Old husband fleeing this person giving us a lift

explanation.walkthrough: 'this person' is not a pointer at the setter; 'this' is a piece and the definition is Elisha Otis, whose company makes lifts, or elevators.

clue.text: Lady wife leaves for the country

indicators.note: someone who leaves goes away

explanation.surface: A lady whose wife moves out to the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves for the country' reads as a trip out of town; 'leaves' only drops the W.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a sultanate on the Arabian Peninsula.

clue.text: Stylish welcome received in clubs twice

indicators.note: a guest received in a house is taken inside

blocks.note: C = clubs, the card suit, written twice

explanation.surface: A stylish greeting given at two nightclubs.

explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym borrowed from French: elegant and fashionable.

clue.text: Champion one foreign people must embrace

indicators.note: to embrace someone is to wrap your arms round them

explanation.surface: A champion from abroad whom the locals must welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foreign' goes with 'one', not 'people': UN is French for one.

clue.text: Writer in fictional realm wanting start in Republic

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: the writer of the clue, the setter, is me
NARNIA, C. S. Lewis's magic land, without its N

explanation.surface: An author stuck in a fantasy world, lacking a start in the Republic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' is the setter, ME, not a novelist, though Narnia tempts one to look for C. S. Lewis.

clue.text: Ottoman officer edges away from infidel

indicators.note: the edges are a word's outer letters

explanation.surface: A Turkish officer sidling away from an unbeliever.

explanation.definitionFit: A historical title: a military commander in the Ottoman Empire.

clue.text: Rapidly consumes cool hotel beers

blocks.note: H is hotel in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone downing cold beers at a hotel bar.

clue.text: Special expert with a Liberal leader venturing forth from Atlantis?

explanation.walkthrough: 'Atlantis' is not the sunken city but a NASA space shuttle; the question mark flags the switch.

clue.text: Historic document: Reform Act with anagram!
